analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage lenders to verify borrowers can repay and bans bonuses for steering people into bad loans.
analysis.headline: The House passed the mortgage reform bill 291–127 on November 15, 2007, but the Senate committee never acted and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required mortgage lenders to check, with documented income information, that a borrower can actually repay a home loan before making it. It would have banned paying loan officers bonuses for steering borrowers into more expensive loans, required licensing and background checks for loan originators, restricted prepayment penalties and balloon payments, and created a HUD office to fund housing counseling. It passed the House in November 2007, as the subprime crisis was unfolding, but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and homeowners, especially subprime borrowers with adjustable-rate mortgages, and people facing foreclosure; also housing counseling organizations and independent appraisers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires creditors to verify, with documented income and debt information, that a borrower can repay a loan under its full terms including taxes and insurance, and to count future rate increases on adjustable and interest-only loans when doing so.

Prohibits paying loan originators incentive compensation that varies with a loan's terms, the arrangement that rewarded pushing borrowers into costlier loans, and directs regulators to bar steering borrowers into loans they cannot repay or that carry predatory terms.

Requires a nationwide licensing system for mortgage loan originators with background checks, 20 hours of pre-licensing education, a written test, and a public registry of each originator's employment and disciplinary history.

Restricts prepayment penalties, bans balloon payments on high-cost mortgages, bars single-premium credit insurance and mandatory arbitration clauses, and prohibits refinancings that give the borrower no net benefit.

Requires a certified counselor's sign-off before a high-cost mortgage is made, creates a HUD Office of Housing Counseling with grants, and gives borrowers a defense to foreclosure when a loan violated the ability-to-repay rules.
Requires lenders to obtain independent appraisals, give borrowers a free copy three days before closing, and prohibits pressuring appraisers to hit a target value.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers, lenders, securitizers, and servicers, who would face licensing costs, liability, banned fee arrangements, and tighter servicing rules; bank employees get a lighter registration standard than independent brokers.

drawbacks.text: The licensing system creates a two-tier playing field: employees of banks and credit unions need only to register with federal agencies, while independent mortgage brokers must obtain full state licenses, pass a 100-question test, and complete 20 hours of education, adding cost and pushing business toward banks.

The bill significantly softens the punch against Wall Street: assignees and securitizers face liability only for rescission, can avoid liability by curing a loan or meeting a due-diligence checklist, cannot be sued in class actions, are exempted for loans placed in securitization pools, and the bill overrides state laws that provide stronger remedies against them.

Requiring certified counseling before any high-cost mortgage could add delays and paperwork for exactly the lower-income borrowers the bill is trying to protect, and the bill itself directs a study of its effects on the availability and affordability of mortgage credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — verified ability to repay, no bonuses for steering, honest appraisals, limits on prepayment penalties — target the specific practices that were producing unaffordable loans and foreclosures. The costs to the industry are real but mostly the expense of doing what the bill considered basic underwriting. The honest trade-offs are the bank-versus-broker double standard in licensing and the carve-outs that shielded securitizers and investors from full liability, which shows how far the compromise reached by the time the House voted.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 291–127 in November 2007, but the Senate referred it to its Banking Committee on December 3, 2007, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before that Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Brad Miller introduced the bill on October 22, 2007, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
The committee marked it up on November 6, ordered it reported by voice vote, and reported it amended on November 9, 2007.
A Republican motion to recommit with instructions failed 188–231 on November 15, 2007, with 10 Democrats and 178 Republicans in favor.
The House passed the bill 291–127 on November 15, 2007, with all 232 voting Democrats in favor and Republicans split 64 for, 127 against.

The Senate received the bill on December 3, 2007, and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action appears in the record through the end of the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders, brokers, securitizers, and servicers, who kept operating under the pre-reform rules through the 2008 housing collapse; borrowers got none of the protections until far more foreclosures had already happened.

for.name: Brad Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the House.

for.name: Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Managed the bill through committee markup and floor consideration, including his own amendment and the procedural motion to move the bill forward.

against.name: Marsha Blackburn
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions adding an approved-identification requirement for mortgage applicants; the motion failed 188–231.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration or a Senate floor vote on the bill after it was referred on December 3, 2007.

sides.party_line_note: House passage was 291–127: every voting Democrat supported it (227–0), while Republicans split 64 in favor and 127 against; a Republican motion to recommit drew near-unanimous Republican support and failed 188–231.

industries.note: The bill bans the yield-spread premiums and steering bonuses that paid originators more for putting borrowers in costlier loans, and adds full state licensing, testing, and liability up to three times their compensation on a loan. Their profits depended on arrangements the bill would make illegal or risky.

industries.industry: Mortgage securitizers and investors in mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: The bill puts them on the hook for rescission of loans that violated the underwriting rules, but the House version also bans class actions against them, exempts loans in securitization pools and their investors, lets them escape liability through a due-diligence policy, and overrides stronger state remedies. Even as written, the liability is far lighter than what borrowers could pursue under state law.

industries.industry: Depository institutions (banks and their mortgage arms)
industries.note: Their employees get a lighter federal registration instead of full state licensing, giving banks an advantage over independent brokers, but they still face duty-of-care, ability-to-repay, and escrow requirements. The playing field tilts toward banks while everyone is regulated.

The bill requires escrow accounts for taxes and insurance, restricts force-placed insurance, requires prompt crediting of payments and faster responses to borrower error claims, and raises damages for violations. These rules target the servicing practices that added fees and pushed borrowers toward default.

The bill creates a HUD Office of Housing Counseling, funds counseling grants, and requires certified counseling before high-cost mortgages, routing new public money and mandatory demand to these nonprofits.

The bill protects appraiser independence from lender pressure, gives state regulators federal grants, and raises annual registry fees from $25 to $40. Appraisers gain standing and funding at modest cost.
